Description of Event: Global oil supply disruptions led to widespread stagflation and high inflation in Australia, exposing the inefficiencies and rising costs of the state-owned energy monopolies 1.

Severe drought reduced water availability necessary for hydro-electric generators and the cooling systems of coal plants 2. This constrained supply during periods of high heatwave demand, spiking wholesale prices 2.

The global credit crunch elevated the cost of debt 3. Under the regulatory pricing model used by the Australian Energy Regulator, network businesses were allowed to recover these higher debt costs from consumers, heavily driving up retail bills 3.

Extreme weather events physically destroyed local powerlines and infrastructure, causing extended consumer outages (such as regional Queensland customers experiencing an average of 1,391 minutes off supply during Yasi) 4-6.
Catastrophic thunderstorms and destructive winds caused major network failures, leading to a complete state-wide blackout 7, 8.
Pandemic lockdowns temporarily reduced electricity demand and pushed wholesale prices down 9, 10. Concurrently, COVID-19 restrictions disrupted supply chains and plant maintenance schedules 9, 11.
Heavy rains and flooding closed coal mines and disrupted rail freight 12. This led to a severe under-delivery of fuel to coal-fired power stations during a period of high demand 12.

The conflict sparked a global energy crisis that sent international coal and gas prices to record highs 11, 13. Because Australia's East Coast gas market is linked to global LNG markets, domestic wholesale prices spiked, eventually forcing a temporary suspension of the National Electricity Market (NEM) and the introduction of emergency price caps 11, 13-15.

A major thunderstorm caused six high-voltage transmission towers to collapse, abruptly disconnecting 2,210 megawatts of generation and requiring load shedding that left 90,000 customers without power 7.
